query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation and eventual catastrophic failure in additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA at elevated temperatures is governed by the interplay between the formation of a protective surface oxide scale and internal chemical ingress. In oxidizing conditions (high oxygen partial pressure), a relatively continuous, adherent oxide scale forms that slows further oxygen penetration and internal degradation. Under reducing conditions (low oxygen partial pressure), the absence or discontinuity of this protective scale allows enhanced ingress of oxygen (or hydrogen) into the microstructure, particularly along grain boundaries, which promotes the formation of embrittling phases (such as BCC precipitates) and accelerates catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured, as-built FCC solid solution microstructure of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with minimal pre-existing oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of oxygen partial pressure while maintaining a constant temperature (e.g., 800 °C) and exposure duration (e.g., up to 48 hours); comparing exposures in a standard air (oxidizing) environment with those in a low-O2, reducing gas mixture.
generation.conditions: Temperature range of 700–900 °C with a fixed exposure duration (e.g., 48 hours) while altering oxygen partial pressures from typical air (≈21% O2) to a controlled low oxygen partial pressure environment (e.g., O2 diluted with H2-containing reducing gas mixtures).
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity, composition, and adherence of the surface oxide scale and the degree of grain-boundary phase changes (e.g., formation of embrittling BCC phases) as modulated by gas ingress.
generation.mechanism: At high oxygen partial pressure, the surface rapidly forms a relatively uniform oxide scale that acts as a barrier to further oxygen penetration; however, at elevated temperature and extended exposure, scale spallation may eventually occur. Under reducing conditions, the suppressed formation of a continuous oxide scale allows internal oxygen/hydrogen ingress, particularly along the grain boundaries, which in turn promotes phase transformations (e.g., FCC to brittle BCC) and embrittlement, leading to earlier catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-built state, specimens exposed under oxidizing conditions will develop a thicker, continuous oxide layer with limited internal phase transformation and only gradual deterioration. In contrast, specimens exposed under reducing conditions will show a thinner or discontinuous oxide scale, accelerated formation of embrittling phases along grain boundaries, and a measurable decrease in ductility and toughness (evidenced by earlier catastrophic failure in mechanical testing).
generation.baseline: The as-built HEA state, which exhibits a defect-free FCC microstructure with an initially minimal surface oxide layer and expected stable mechanical properties under modest conditions.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 700–900 °C; Gas composition: from air (≈21% O2, oxidizing) to low-O2/H2-containing reducing atmospheres; Exposure duration: up to 48 hours.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in oxide scale thickness, rates of internal oxygen/hydrogen ingress, and exact thresholds for phase transformation-induced embrittlement are uncertain due to the multicomponent nature of the alloy and complex diffusion kinetics. The interplay between surface oxidation kinetics and internal phase changes may also depend on local processing-induced defects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 specimens. Expose one set to an oxidizing environment (air) and another to a low oxygen partial pressure, reducing gas mixture at a constant temperature (e.g., 800 °C) for 48 hours. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural evaluations (using SEM, TEM, and EDS) of the surface and cross-sectional regions to assess the oxide scale integrity and internal phase changes. In addition, conduct mechanical tensile tests to evaluate ductility and detect early signs of catastrophic failure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM/EDS and XRD)
Identification and quantification of phase transformations (e.g., detection of BCC or embrittling phases) using XRD and TEM
Grain-boundary composition and evidence of internal chemical ingress (by EDS mapping)
Mechanical property assessments such as tensile strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant differences in oxide scale continuity, internal phase composition (particularly embrittling phases), and mechanical failure modes are not observed between specimens exposed to oxidizing versus reducing conditions—i.e., if both environments yield similar oxide scale characteristics and mechanical properties—the hypothesis that degradation is governed by differences in surface oxidation and subsequent internal embrittlement would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The formation of MnO was expected, as Mn is the most reactive element in the alloy mixture to react with oxygen. The fast growth of MnO should be kinetically favourable because of its highly unstable nature. The high-temperature oxidation of Mn to MnO, i.e., 700 °C instead of 550 °C (during HTXRD in air), can be explained by lower oxygen partial pressure. With an increase in oxidation temperature and exposure time, MnO phase peaks’ intensity progressively increased, which indicates Mn’s continuous oxidation. Quantitative analysis of the data revealed a gradual increase in the second phase due to the fast formation of MnO. As Mn has a higher affinity for oxygen, with an increase in temperature, Mn preferentially diffuses from inside to the surface and thus reacts with oxygen. The observed trend in the increase in the phase quantity with time and temperature is in good agreement with parabolic kinetics []. As shown in Figure 5c, the scale thickness formed was extremely low due to lower oxygen partial pressure. As We et al. [] reported, the oxidation rate increases with an increase in oxygen partial pressure during the oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi alloy in varying levels of oxyge

Figure 7c shows the cross-section topography after high-temperature XRD oxidation in air. An irregular oxide scale formed and remained adherent to the substrate. The oxide scale thickness is about 1.58, 2.53, and 3.45 μm at different locations, which indicates that oxidation does not occur uniformly on the surface. Furthermore, no evidence of internal oxidation attack along the grain boundaries within the substrate was observed. In addition, no internal oxidation attack in the substrate is seen as having been executed along the grain boundaries. Figure 8 presents a cross-sectional EDS map of the specimen oxidized when heated during in situ XRD. For the specimen oxidized, it was observed that a mixed oxide layer consisting of Mn, Cr, and Fe oxides on the substrate and the oxides were confirmed to be Mn2O3, Mn3O4, Fe3Mn3O8, and MnCr2O4 when combined with XRD data shown in Figure 6. Mn- and Cr-depleted areas formed in the scale–substrate interface area, which are now filled with a high concentration of Ni, Co, and Fe. Kim et al. AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. While, in the corrosive environment of high-temperature/pressure water, the alloy surface is oxidized by chemical reactions with water and this oxide surface layer can suppress the formation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulting FCC-to-HCP phase transit

verified.quote: what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur

occupying_moves.lever: gas composition (oxygen partial pressure) and temperature
occupying_moves.technique: high-temperature exposure tests with in-situ thermogravimetric analysis and complementary post-exposure SEM/TEM and XRD characterization
occupying_moves.conditions: Exposures at 700–900 °C under precisely controlled oxidizing (e.g., air or 21% O2) versus reducing (e.g., H2/N2 mixture) atmospheres for durations up to 100 hours

chosen.technique: in-situ thermogravimetric analysis during high-temperature exposure combined with ex-situ SEM/TEM and XRD to monitor scale formation and microstructural evolution
chosen.conditions: Exposure tests conducted at temperatures between 700 and 900 °C under systematically varied oxygen partial pressures (contrasting an oxidizing atmosphere with a reducing one) for durations sufficient to capture early stage oxide nucleation to catastrophic failure, benchmarked against the as-manufactured alloy baseline
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question regarding the mechanistic origins of degradation by toggling the gas environment—a key lever governing oxidation kinetics and related microstructural damage. Using standard high-temperature, controlled-variable experiments in the field of materials science, this study is well-poised to directly test the hypothesis that differences in scale formation (or the absence thereof) and induced residual stresses lead to catastrophic failure. The chosen approach removes prevailing simplifications by comparing both oxidizing and reducing environments under identical thermal conditions and tracking the evolution of protective scale formation and failure micro-cracking, thereby providing clear criteria for falsification by deviations from the predicted behavior relative to the starting state.

frame.system: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix in its as-built microstructure.
frame.goal: To understand and verify the mechanistic pathway governing degradation—and ultimately catastrophic failure—under elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases.
frame.limitation: The current state of knowledge does not clearly elucidate whether degradation is primarily driven by surface-scale oxidation/reduction kinetics, internal oxygen/hydrogen ingress, phase boundary embrittlement, or other microstructural changes that lead to failure.
constraints: A controlled change (e.g., systematically varying the oxygen partial pressure or gas composition while keeping temperature constant) must be defined to isolate the responsible mechanism.
The hypothesis must predict clear differences in behavior relative to a well‐characterized baseline state.
Exposure boundaries (temperature range, gas composition/concentration, exposure duration) need to be tightly specified.
Prior evidence in similar FCC high-entropy alloys and oxidation studies should support the proposed mechanism.

A falsification criterion must be established such that if the predicted microstructural and mechanical changes (e.g., oxide scale integrity loss, formation of embrittling phases at grain boundaries) are not observed, the hypothesis is refuted.
frame.regime: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) under controlled atmospheres ranging from oxidizing (e.g., air or high O2 content) to reducing environments (e.g., H2- or CO-containing mixtures).
prior_attempts: Studies on similar high-entropy alloys have observed oxidation-induced phase changes, but without a direct, controlled comparison between oxidizing and reducing regimes.

Conventional investigations often failed to decouple the contributions of external oxide scale degradation from internal microstructural embrittlement, leaving the catastrophic failure mechanism ambiguous.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on high-entropy alloys under elevated-temperature exposure have first focused on how microstructural refinement and processing (e.g., friction processing) can slow oxidation kinetics, as seen in PMC9026100, where ultrafine-grained microstructures showed decelerated oxidation and improved scale formation (chromia/alumina). Later, atomistic simulations (PMC9969177) revealed that the chemical reactivity at the surface under oxidizing environments can alter dislocation activities and phase transformations (e.g., suppressing FCC-to-HCP and instead promoting FCC-to-BCC transitions) that likely tie to embrittlement. In both cases, although oxidation phenomena and phase-change mechanisms were documented, prior work did not clearly decouple whether degradation and eventual catastrophic failure arise primarily from the external oxide scale integrity or from internal oxygen ingress leading to grain-boundary embrittlement.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved whether the key mechanism governing degradation is controlled by surface-scale oxidation–reduction kinetics (e.g., formation and loss of protective oxide layers) or by internal chemical ingress that degrades grain boundaries and triggers catastrophic failure. Specifically, in additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with its as-built microstructure, the interplay between gas composition effects and subtle microstructural transformations has not been isolated.
decision.lever: systematic variation of oxygen partial pressure in the gas environment (while maintaining temperature between 700–900 °C)
decision.why: Based on the trend, earlier investigations demonstrated that oxidation behavior and ensuing phase transformations are sensitive to surface reactions (PMC9026100) while atomistic simulations underscore that the gas environment can alter deformation mechanisms (PMC9969177). A controlled experiment varying the oxygen partial pressure (e.g., running exposures in air versus low-O2/H2-containing reducing mixtures) will directly test whether degradation and failure are governed by external oxide scale changes or by internal oxygen/hydrogen ingress. The hypothesis is that lowering oxygen partial pressure will diminish the formation of a protective oxide scale, leading instead to more pronounced internal embrittlement (or vice versa), and the predicted outcomes (changes in oxide scale integrity, variation in grain-boundary phases, reduced ductility relative to the as-built baseline) will serve as clear criteria for falsification if not observed under the specified conditions.
